question.:question/worked-solution:
To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(\frac{1}{15})}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{(\frac{1}{15})}^{x}}{\ln (\frac{1}{15})}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\ln (\frac{1}{15}) & =\ln 1-\ln 15 \\  & =0-\ln 15 \\  & =-\ln 15.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(\frac{1}{15})}^{x}}{\ln (\frac{1}{15})}+C=-\frac{{(\frac{1}{15})}^{x}}{\ln 15}+C\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: real x; logarithmic distractors compared on x>0; arbitrary additive C
